distillation_scope_note: Pure disease-name distillation: Chronic myeloid leukemia blast crisis. Blast lineage, prior TKI exposure, resistance mutations, cytogenetics, BCR-ABL confirmation, and marrow or flow results are represented as confirmatory or treatment-context modifiers, not as ordinary presentation observations.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Constitutive ABL1 kinase signaling sustains the CML clone, myeloproliferation, splenic extramedullary hematopoiesis, genomic instability, and TKI-sensitive disease pressure.

The chronic-phase substrate of left-shifted granulocytosis, basophilia, thrombocytosis or platelet dysregulation, and splenomegaly remains clinically visible in many blast-crisis presentations and helps separate CML blast crisis from de novo AML/ALL or leukemoid reaction.

Acquired genetic and epigenetic lesions create a severe block in differentiation and apoptosis, converting CML into an acute-leukemia-like state with myeloid, lymphoid, mixed, or rare megakaryoblastic blast phenotypes.
Expanded blasts in marrow and blood drive blast fraction, hyperleukocytosis, LDH elevation, marrow failure, leukostasis, tumor lysis pressure, and early mortality.

Blast replacement, ineffective CML hematopoiesis, fibrosis, and treatment effects suppress normal erythroid, megakaryocytic, and neutrophil production, producing anemia, thrombocytopenia or dysfunctional thrombocytosis, infection risk, and bleeding.

High circulating blast count and adhesive blasts obstruct pulmonary, cerebral, retinal, renal, and cardiac microcirculation, causing dyspnea, hypoxemia, neurologic deficits, ocular symptoms, renal injury, and rapid death.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: High cell-turnover and tumor lysis pressure
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: High blast and granulocytic turnover, amplified by cytoreduction or induction therapy, releases uric acid, phosphate, potassium, and LDH, creating AKI, arrhythmia, seizure, and metabolic death risk.
Blasts may infiltrate lymph nodes, spleen, liver, skin, bone, CNS, orbit/retina, serosa, or other tissues, producing focal organ mimicry beyond ordinary leukocytosis.

Thrombocytopenia, dysfunctional extreme thrombocytosis, leukemic endothelial activation, infection overlap, or DIC-like consumption can cause mucosal bleeding, soft tissue bleeding, elevated D-dimer, and fatal hemorrhage.

Marrow failure, dysfunctional myeloid immunity, steroids, induction chemotherapy, TKI effects, catheters, and mucosal injury increase febrile neutropenia, sepsis, and fungal infection risk; infection can overlap with leukemia fever.

Kinase-domain mutations, additional chromosomal abnormalities, high-risk fusion partners, adherence gaps, or pharmacologic underexposure reduce TKI control and allow blast-crisis geometry to persist despite BCR-ABL-directed therapy.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: BCR-ABL1 signaling creates the chronic CML substrate of left-shifted myeloproliferation and splenic disease.
Persistent BCR-ABL1 activity promotes genomic instability and acquisition of blast-crisis-driving lesions.
Resistant clones keep BCR-ABL pathway activity high despite nominal TKI exposure.
Resistance lowers the probability that a selected TKI will adequately reshape the BCR-ABL clone.
Treatment resistance is the observable context form of resistant clonal activity.
Differentiation arrest and clonal evolution generate expanded blast populations.
Blast phenotype can be myeloid, lymphoid, mixed, or rare megakaryoblastic; lineage probability belongs to confirmatory treatment context.
Lymphoid blast-crisis biology changes chemotherapy and CNS-risk context but should not be injected into ordinary presentation observations.
CML background commonly produces leukocytosis independent of blast fraction.
Myelocytes, metamyelocytes, promyelocytes, and a full granulocytic spectrum point toward CML-background myeloproliferation rather than pure de novo acute leukemia.
Basophilia is a useful ordinary differentiator from leukemoid reaction and many de novo acute leukemias, although it can be absent in some blast-crisis presentations.
Absolute basophilia integrates WBC count and differential fraction.
CML background and megakaryocytic crisis can produce thrombocytosis, while marrow failure and consumption can produce thrombocytopenia.
Splenic extramedullary hematopoiesis and leukemic infiltration are common CML-background features.
High peripheral blast percentage is a direct ordinary expression of blast crisis when available on smear or differential.
Absolute blast count captures both WBC count and blast fraction and better tracks leukostasis pressure than either alone.
Marrow blast percentage confirms blast crisis but should be stored as hematopathology or confirmatory context in cases.
High proliferation, tissue ischemia, and cell turnover elevate LDH.
Marrow blast expansion suppresses normal hematopoiesis.
Anemia is common from marrow replacement, ineffective erythropoiesis, bleeding, and treatment effects.
Normal neutrophil output can be reduced despite high total WBC dominated by blasts or immature cells.
Anemia and systemic leukemia burden commonly present as fatigue, weakness, and poor performance status.
Neutrophil dysfunction, neutropenia, mucosal injury, and therapy-induced aplasia increase infection risk.
Fever can reflect infection, leukemia inflammation, or treatment-associated febrile neutropenia.
Measured fever is common but not required; steroids or severe illness can blunt temperature.
CRP rises with infection, leukemia inflammation, tissue necrosis, and DIC overlap.
Infection hazards are decisive during presentation, induction, aplasia, transplant, and corticosteroid exposure.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Risk is highest with high circulating blast count and pulmonary, neurologic, ocular, renal, or cardiac symptoms.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Circulating blasts create microvascular obstruction and endothelial injury.
Symptomatic leukostasis is the event-level expression of blast microvascular obstruction.
Pulmonary leukostasis, anemia, infection, or DIC can present as dyspnea.
Pulmonary microvascular obstruction and infection overlap lower oxygenation.
CNS leukostasis, hemorrhage, infection, or leukemic infiltration can cause encephalopathy, seizure, or focal deficits.
Pulmonary leukostasis, infection, hemorrhage, or volume stress can rapidly progress to respiratory failure.
High burden and cytotoxic therapy increase cell turnover and metabolic release.
Purine catabolism raises uric acid before and during cytoreduction.
Cell lysis releases intracellular potassium.
Cell lysis raises phosphate.
Calcium may fall through calcium-phosphate precipitation during tumor lysis.
Urate nephropathy, sepsis, leukostasis, nephrotoxic drugs, or dehydration can cause AKI.
High turnover and cytoreduction create clinical TLS risk.
High blast burden and lineage biology increase tissue infiltration risk.
Extramedullary leukemia is the clinical expression of tissue blast infiltration.
Lymphoid or extramedullary blast crisis can involve nodes.
Liver involvement can reflect CML myeloproliferation, leukemic infiltration, or extramedullary hematopoiesis.
Retinal, choroidal, or optic involvement can present with decreased vision or serous retinal detachment.
Ocular leukemic involvement or leukostasis may produce blurred or decreased vision.
CNS infiltration may occur, particularly in lymphoid blast crisis or relapse contexts.
Splenomegaly, hepatic involvement, infarction, or extramedullary masses can produce abdominal pain or fullness.
Skin involvement, paraneoplastic inflammation, infection, drug exposure, or nonspecific rash can accompany blast-crisis presentations.
Fibrin turnover raises D-dimer when DIC-like coagulopathy develops.
Fibrinogen may fall when consumption exceeds acute-phase production.
Blast crisis can develop DIC-like physiology, especially with infection, high burden, or tissue-factor biology.
Low or dysfunctional platelets and coagulopathy raise major bleeding risk.
Severe leukostasis rapidly drives respiratory, neurologic, renal, or cardiac fatality.
TLS causes AKI, arrhythmia, seizure, and metabolic death risk.
Sepsis, pneumonia, and invasive fungal disease are major death paths during blast crisis and induction.
Persistent blast burden predicts treatment failure, early complications, and relapse mortality.

axes.clinical_interpretation: Fever can arise from leukemia inflammation, infection, transfusion, TLS, DIC, or treatment-related neutropenia; it is not a confirmatory CML marker.
Reported fever helps separate infectious or inflammatory presentation from purely hematologic presentation but is nonspecific.
Often reflects anemia, hypercatabolism, splenomegaly, infection, or treatment failure.
Subacute catabolic symptoms support malignancy biology but overlap with infection, lymphoma, HLH, and other inflammatory diseases.
A malignant or infectious B-symptom-like axis, not specific to CML blast crisis.
CML blast crisis can present with hyperleukocytosis, normal WBC, or leukopenic blast crisis; interpret with blast fraction, differential, and cytopenias.
Ordinary smear or differential blast percentage is a high-value presentation axis for blast crisis and for AML/ALL mimic clustering.
Combines WBC and blast fraction; important for leukostasis and TLS pressure.
Bone marrow blast percentage confirms blast crisis but should be stored in hematopathology or confirmatory_findings in cases, not ordinary observations.
Left-shifted granulocytic maturation supports CML-background biology and helps distinguish leukemoid reaction or de novo AML/ALL when interpreted with basophils and blasts.
Basophilia supports CML over leukemoid reaction but can be absent in some blast-crisis cases.
Absolute basophilia is a robust CML-background differentiator when available.
ANC can be high from granulocytosis or low from marrow failure/therapy; interpret separately from total WBC.
Anemia is common and contributes to fatigue, dyspnea, and poor tolerance of induction therapy.
Platelets may be very low from marrow failure or very high/dysfunctional from CML and megakaryoblastic biology.
LDH tracks cell turnover, tissue ischemia, leukostasis, TLS, and tumor burden.
Elevated uric acid indicates high turnover or TLS pressure and modifies prophylaxis urgency.
CRP can reflect infection, leukemia inflammation, tissue necrosis, DIC, or treatment complications; it does not by itself distinguish sepsis from leukemia fever.
Renal injury may come from TLS, leukostasis, sepsis, dehydration, nephrotoxins, or baseline CKD.
Hyperkalemia is a TLS and renal-failure hazard axis.
Hyperphosphatemia tracks TLS pressure.
Hypocalcemia may emerge during TLS and contributes to seizure or arrhythmia risk.
D-dimer rises with DIC-like coagulopathy, thrombosis, infection, tissue necrosis, or leukostasis.
May be low from consumption or high as an acute-phase reactant; interpret with D-dimer and bleeding.
A major CML-background differentiator; can cause early satiety, abdominal distension, and pain.
Reflects extramedullary hematopoiesis, leukemic infiltration, congestion, or infection overlap.
Can support lymphoid or extramedullary blast crisis but overlaps lymphoma and infection.
May come from massive spleen, hepatomegaly, infarction, infection, or extramedullary disease.
Can reflect marrow expansion, infarction, extramedullary disease, infection, or drug effects.
Nonspecific axis for leukemia cutis, infection, drug eruption, or inflammatory mimic; pathology confirmation should stay separate.
Can represent anemia, pulmonary leukostasis, infection, DIC/hemorrhage, heart disease, or volume overload.
Low oxygenation raises concern for pulmonary leukostasis, pneumonia, hemorrhage, or cardiopulmonary comorbidity.
Can be leukostasis, CNS involvement, sepsis, TLS, hemorrhage, or drug toxicity.
Blurred or decreased vision can reflect ocular leukemic involvement, retinal vascular injury, hemorrhage, or unrelated ophthalmic disease.
Clinical or imaging suspicion of tissue blast disease; tissue pathology remains confirmatory.
Retinal/choroidal or optic involvement is uncommon but important; ophthalmic imaging can be ordinary organ evidence while leukemia confirmation stays separate.
Neurologic or CSF context for CNS disease; CSF cytology/flow is confirmatory.

axes.display_name: Acute respiratory failure hazard in CML blast crisis
axes.clinical_interpretation: Respiratory failure can emerge from leukostasis, infection, hemorrhage, TLS volume stress, transfusion, or cardiac disease.

axes.display_name: Tumor lysis syndrome hazard in CML blast crisis
axes.clinical_interpretation: TLS risk rises with high burden, renal impairment, dehydration, and rapid cytoreduction.
Bacterial/fungal infection hazard from marrow failure, chemotherapy, catheters, steroids, and mucosal injury.
DIC-like coagulopathy can occur but is less defining than in APL; it should not be overused as a subtype label.
Driven by severe thrombocytopenia, dysfunctional platelets, DIC, leukostasis injury, invasive procedures, or treatment aplasia.
Treatment history context that changes resistance probability and practical TKI selection.
Resistance context from treatment failure, kinase mutation, or cytogenetic evolution; do not invent it from ordinary labs alone.
Molecular treatment context that strongly modifies TKI choice and expected response.
Treatment-context probability derived from mutation, prior exposure, adherence, interactions, and cytogenetic evolution; not a presentation observation.
Flow/morphology/cytochemistry context that modifies chemotherapy vector field; store flow/cytochemistry in confirmatory_findings.
Flow/morphology context for lymphoid blast crisis and CNS-risk management; not ordinary presentation evidence.
Access, hemodynamic stability, leukostasis urgency, and center capability modify leukapheresis use.
Age, frailty, organ function, infection, and patient goals change net induction vector value.

axes.display_name: Allogeneic transplant eligibility in CML blast crisis
axes.clinical_interpretation: Donor availability, remission status, infection, organ function, and frailty determine transplant feasibility.
Monitoring, fluids, urate lowering, dialysis access, and renal/cardiac reserve modify cytoreduction safety.
Modifies chemotherapy, steroid, transplant, and antimicrobial net effects.
Blood product availability and refractoriness modify marrow-failure and bleeding support.
Renal impairment modifies TLS prophylaxis, antimicrobial dosing, TKI choice, chemotherapy, and transplant risk.

axes.display_name: Mortality hazard in CML blast crisis
axes.clinical_interpretation: Lifespan outcome hazard integrating blast persistence, leukostasis, TLS, infection, bleeding/DIC, organ failure, treatment response, and transplant feasibility.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Stronger when peripheral_blood_blast_fraction and circulating_blast_count are high; weaker when leukocytosis is mostly mature granulocytes.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: WBC alone is insufficient, but high WBC contributes to leukostasis pressure in blast crisis.
Absolute circulating blast count is the most direct ordinary quantitative driver of leukostasis risk.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Highest during cytoreduction, TKI response, induction chemotherapy, renal dysfunction, dehydration, or high LDH/uric acid.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: High blast fraction increases cell-kill substrate for TLS.
Hyperuricemia is a measurable TLS pressure axis.
Renal impairment lowers clearance of uric acid, phosphate, and potassium and raises TLS mortality.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Risk rises when platelet count is very low; extreme thrombocytosis may also be dysfunctional but is not equivalent to hemostatic safety.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Severe thrombocytopenia is a direct bleeding risk axis.
DIC-like consumption amplifies major bleeding risk beyond platelet count alone.
Major bleeding and procedure-related hemorrhage raise early mortality.
Respiratory failure from leukostasis, infection, hemorrhage, or volume stress is a major early death path.
Infection and sepsis drive death during blast crisis and treatment aplasia.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Correlation weakens with corticosteroids, profound marrow failure, or noninfectious TLS/DIC-driven inflammation.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever and CRP often co-vary through inflammatory cytokines but should not be treated as a causal edge.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Present when CML-background myeloproliferation remains visible; may be absent in overt acute lymphoid blast crisis.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Basophilia and granulocytic left shift share the CML-background mechanism.
Massive spleen can cause abdominal distension, early satiety, pain, or infarct symptoms.
Ocular leukemic involvement can cause decreased vision, retinal detachment, hemorrhage, or vascular occlusion.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Mutation and exposure context determine whether BCR-ABL inhibition can suppress the clone.
T315I makes many TKIs ineffective while preserving activity for selected agents.
Resistant clones reduce expected blast and CML-background response.

side_effects.interpretation: Myelosuppression and combination therapy can increase infection risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: BCR-ABL vector reshaping whose net value depends on molecular sensitivity and must usually be paired with blast-lineage cytoreduction or transplant pathway decisions.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cytoreduction without monitoring or urate/electrolyte control can worsen TLS risk.
Renal dysfunction raises TLS and dosing constraints.

side_effects.interpretation: Cytoreduction can worsen thrombocytopenia or marrow suppression.

treatments.context_specific_role: Short-interval count and leukostasis-pressure control while confirmatory context and definitive disease-directed therapy are organized.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Procedural count reduction has greatest causal value when symptomatic leukostasis is active.
Feasibility and stability determine whether leukapheresis can be delivered safely and fast enough.

present.trajectory_modulation: Infection can mimic sepsis/HLH and complicate induction timing; do not erase leukemia evidence when cultures are negative.

supportive_care: Use ordinary presentation observations first: symptoms, vitals, CBC with differential, peripheral blast fraction, WBC/blast count, hemoglobin, platelets, LDH, uric acid, creatinine, potassium, phosphate, calcium, CRP, D-dimer/fibrinogen when available, spleen/liver/nodal/ocular/CNS/respiratory involvement, and infection evaluation.

Keep BCR-ABL1 PCR/FISH, Philadelphia chromosome, marrow blast percentage, marrow morphology, flow cytometry, cytogenetics, and kinase-domain mutations in confirmatory_findings or treatment-context axes. They should not be ordinary ranking observations unless explicitly marked use_in_ranking:false.

Separate blast crisis from de novo AML/ALL by ordinary CML-background signals when available: basophilia, full granulocytic left shift, splenomegaly, prior CML course, and thrombocytosis or platelet dysregulation. Confirmation still requires BCR-ABL/Ph-context evidence.

Separate leukemoid reaction from CML blast crisis by blast fraction/count, basophils, left-shift pattern, spleen size, LDH/uric acid, cytopenias, and absence or presence of infection-source evidence; do not use culture or molecular confirmation as ordinary shortcut evidence.

Separate sepsis, HLH, and inflammatory mimics by preserving fever, CRP, ferritin, organ dysfunction, cytopenias, cultures, source imaging, and infection exclusions as their own axes rather than deleting leukemia evidence.
Monitor urgently for leukostasis when high circulating blasts accompany dyspnea, hypoxemia, neurologic change, visual symptoms, renal injury, or chest/cardiac symptoms.
Start TLS prevention and frequent renal/electrolyte monitoring before and during hydroxyurea, TKI response, leukapheresis, or induction chemotherapy in high-burden disease.
Provide RBC, platelet, fibrinogen/plasma, and ICU support according to anemia, bleeding, DIC-like coagulopathy, respiratory failure, shock, and procedure needs.
Evaluate and treat fever or suspected infection promptly while maintaining leukemia fever and treatment-related fever as competing explanations when microbiology and source workup are unrevealing.
Do not encode static treatment rank labels; TKI, cytoreduction, induction, CNS-directed therapy, transplant, and supportive care should rank by forward simulation under the patient's context.
